chunks: From him, from Hamdawayh, from Muhammad ibn al-Husayn, from al-Hasan ibn Mahbub, from Abd al-Aziz, from Abd Allah ibn Abi Ya'fur, from Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him) who said:

I asked him about a man who stood for an obligatory prayer and prayed one rak'ah while intending it to be a voluntary prayer. He said: 'It is the one you stood for and to which you are committed.' He also said: 'When you stand intending the obligatory prayer and doubt arises later, you are considered to be in the obligatory prayer according to what you initially stood for. And if you entered it while intending a voluntary prayer, then later you intend it to be obligatory, you are considered to be in the voluntary prayer. And only what the servant began with at the start of his prayer is counted for him.'
ai.seo_question: How does one resolve doubt in prayer when the initial intention is unclear or changes?
ai.summary: This hadith from *Tahdhib al-Ahkam* establishes the principle of 'stability of the initial state' (istishab al-awwal) in resolving doubt during prayer, a cornerstone of Shia fiqh. It clarifies that the legal status of the prayer is anchored to the intention held at the moment of commencement, ensuring that subsequent doubts or changes in intention do not invalidate the foundational act. This ruling provides practical certainty for worshippers, preventing excessive doubt (waswas) from disrupting the validity of their obligatory or voluntary prayers.
